source.title: What is Missing? Explaining Neurons Activated by Absent Concepts
source.authors: Robin Hesse; Simone Schaub-Meyer; Jan-Timo Hesse; B. Schiele; Stefan Roth

page_placements.theme: Explanations fitted to top-activating examples (of SAE features, vision units and some neurons) predict activation over the rest of the range only partly

record.file_problem: None; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies encoded absences in image-classification networks, not whether neuron explanations have one main job or the Qwen3 audit shares. Its results are relevant to neuron-level analysis but do not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own measurements of channel activation under inserted patches, the fraction of units affected by inhibitory patches, and prediction flip rates. These bear on neuron-level analysis but measure encoded absence, not the interpretability shares or explanation-prediction accuracy named in the versions; they are recorded under fits_no_version. Prior-work results mentioned in the paper are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether ImageNet vision models (VGG19, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) encode concept absences, using patch insertion, minimization-based feature visualization and non-target attribution. It does not audit neuron-job shares, study language models, revisit InceptionV1 cat-and-car, build neuron attribution graphs, or score explanations by simulating activations. It mentions polysemanticity and superposition only in passing (Appendix A.4, Fig. 11) and does not cite either original source. So it bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that encoded absences are common in ImageNet classifiers, especially for fine-grained classification. Standard attribution and maximization-based feature visualization miss them, while non-target attribution and minimization reveal them. Accounting for absences improves debiasing.
record.recipe_differences: This paper studies vision-model channels using minimization-based patch selection, patch insertion, and attribution; it does not audit language-model neuron explanations on held-out activating text.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured suppression varies by ResNet-50 layer: the authors describe stronger differences in the first and last tested blocks and smaller differences in intermediate blocks. Results are also reported for different patch sizes and image counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Most final-layer channels or neurons are significantly suppressed by least-activating patches relative to random patches: 512/512 in VGG19, 2036/2048 in ResNet-50 and 615/768 in ViT-B/16. Explanations from most-activating patches miss this inhibition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanations of image-model neurons built only from maximally activating inputs omit inhibitory (encoded-absence) functions that most units have. This is related to, but distinct from, V6's claim about predicting where a neuron fires.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet-50, inserting least-activating patches flips predictions more often than random patches: 84% vs 8%, and 8.2% vs 3.5% when suppression only is allowed. Selected patches also yield larger negative attributions (178.25 vs 112.44).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Encoded absences in image-model neurons causally affect predictions.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet-50 channels 2026 and 1470 are suppressed by patches from several different classes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some image-model channels encode the absence of multiple concepts.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The activation results use patch insertions as approximations to ideal concept interventions, which the authors acknowledge. The qualitative channel examples include manual selection of a monosemantic subset of patches, which the authors note may make the examples seem more monosemantic than the full patch sets. The measurements concern image-classification models and do not test the claim versions about language-model neuron-job shares or explanation accuracy on held-out text.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were omitted as claim-relevant rows. The paper's toy-model and debiasing accuracy tables concern encoded-absence demonstrations or debiasing performance, not the claim versions about neuron-job shares or explanation scoring.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or of one-job, two-job or unexplained shares.
No language models and no cross-model or cross-scale shares of neuron jobs.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis and no test of recursive generalization against superposition. The multi-concept absence channels in Fig. 11 are not framed as a test of either.
No interpretable-neuron shares and no comparison across architectures, regularization or tools.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with a replacement model.
No test of whether activating-example explanations predict where held-out activations occur.
No simulation-based scoring of explanations and no comparison of explainer models.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation, tranche and row links are acceptable and no row fixes are needed. R4, R9 and R13 are marked 'absent' in the sense of no suppression beyond random patches; this is fine because they link to no version. Possible thematic relevance to V6 (explanations from activating examples being incomplete) is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test, because the measure is inhibition rather than predictive accuracy of explanations.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate shares with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood poles.
Does not compare neuron-job shares across language models, dense or mixture-of-experts models, or model scales.
Does not revisit the InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or test recursive generalization against superposition.
Does not measure interpretable-neuron shares or test whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain the proposed InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Does not build attribution graphs or compare neuron-based explanations with a trained replacement model.
Does not test whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict activations on held-out examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text or compare explainer models.

relation.reason: It discusses neuron explanation methods and polysemanticity (A.4) but does not test any claim version. The synthesis correctly files it under unfit themes.

tranche.reason: This study is about whether ImageNet vision models encode absences. It does not measure neuron-job shares, LM neurons, InceptionV1 cat-and-car or how well explanations predict activations. It neither tests nor uses the claim.

source_check.notes: Table 1 averages over the 100 top-activating images per unit, with a 48x48 patch in a random corner. ViT uses the minimum over tokens, not CLS. Table 3 gives across-unit SDs for CNNs only (VGG19 least 0.94 ± 1.16; ResNet-50 0.03 ± 0.11). For the 512/512 etc. counts, the significance test, alpha and multiple-comparison correction are not stated.
